speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For a start, I rise to support the Info-communications Media Development Authority (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   In this digital age, how do we ensure that the flow of information is fair, that market competition is orderly and that the public interest is protected?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill is close to our daily lives.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In the past, we drew clear distinctions between media, such as newspapers and magazines, and telecommunications services, such as telephone lines, mobile networks and broadband.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A smartphone is no longer just a communication tool – it is also a news portal, an entertainment platform, an advertising channel and even a starting point for doing business.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A single platform can simultaneously influence content distribution, user choices, advertising revenue, business visibility and public discourse.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The media industry today, therefore, is no longer a purely content-driven industry.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, it has become a "digital highway." Whoever controls the entry points and key resources can influence competition and can also shape what the public sees and how they understand the world.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In real life, no one distinguishes between a "media issue" and a "telecommunications issue." What people care about is: why am I seeing this content?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Why are certain platforms growing ever more dominant?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: From a business perspective, whether the market is fair affects innovation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For consumers, whether choices are adequate affects everyday experience.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For society, whether the information ecosystem is healthy affects public trust.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we continue to apply the old, separate frameworks to today's converged market, it is like using an outdated map to navigate a new city – we will easily lose our way.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: An ordinary business transaction is a commercial matter.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But when it involves a significant media platform, it is no longer just about business – it also concerns the flow of information and public interest.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is like a community with only one main road – if the management changes, it could affect how everyone gets around.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I also support reducing unnecessary burdens even as we strengthen regulation.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some involve only formalities with no change in actual control, and these can be handled through a notification process.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Good regulation is not about more being better – it is about being precise, clear and predictable.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Fourth, the management of key resources is very important.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a small number of parties control resources that are difficult to replicate and the rules of access are unfair, the market will lose its dynamism.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Like a bridge that everyone needs to use, the rules governing it must be fair and transparent.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While this is a fairly strong power, it is not an entirely new concept.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I support the Government retaining such a tool.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: There are situations where, if the market structure itself has given rise to serious problems, ordinary directions or financial penalties may simply not be enough.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That said, I hope that in exercising this power, three principles continue to be upheld.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, it should be used as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, the process should be clear, the reasons well-founded and affected parties given a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Markets need regulation, but they also need certainty.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is especially true for Singapore as an international business hub.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many investors choose Singapore precisely because our institutions are clear, our laws are stable and our regulators are credible.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We must protect competition – but we must also protect confidence in our institutions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Sixth, I also support the inclusion of review and appeal mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Regulation must not only carry authority; it must also be accompanied by due process and oversight.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only then will businesses have confidence and the public have trust.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I have a few questions and suggestions for consideration.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is particularly important in the context of corporate investments, mergers and acquisitions, equity restructuring and business acquisitions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Clear guidance would help reduce uncertainty for businesses navigating these situations.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, for transactions that do not require prior approval but must be notified to IMDA, will the relevant subsidiary legislation set out clearer categories and examples?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If practical case illustrations are provided, businesses will find it much easier to comply.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, can IMDA prepare a plain-language guide specifically for small- and medium-sized media enterprises and emerging digital media companies?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Large corporations typically have legal and compliance teams, but smaller businesses may not have the resources to work through complex provisions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For rules to be effective, people must first be able to understand them and act on them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Regulation should not only prevent problems; it should also give healthy, well-run businesses the confidence to grow.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today's digital ecosystem is like a large marketplace.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A good marketplace is not one without rules.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is one where the rules are clear and fairly enforced, where large players can grow, small operators have a chance and consumers can participate with confidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As the saying goes, "Clear waters let fish swim freely; clear rules give people peace of mind." When market rules are clear, competition thrives.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When regulatory boundaries are well-defined, businesses have confidence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When the public interest is safeguarded, society has trust.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): Beyond these provisions, the Bill also needs to be seen in a broader global context.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Around the world, regulators are grappling with similar challenges, such as how to deal with powerful digital platforms while keeping markets open and innovative.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore must continue to take a calibrated approach.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: What people see online is often shaped by automated systems with recommendation engines ranking models and content creation tools.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: These systems are not always visible, but they are very powerful.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, moving forward, issues like transparency, accountability and trust in these systems will become increasingly important.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A healthy media ecosystem is not just about a strong major player but also about diversity – diversity of voices strengthens innovations and it strengthens public disclosure.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: An informed and discerning public is just as important.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Media literacy and digital awareness are long-term safeguards.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Unlike many other industries, the regulation of media companies is not only about economics, it is fundamentally about the role media plays in society.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Media companies shape public discourse and influence how citizens understand and form opinions.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For these reasons, competition rules in the media sector are essential not just to ensure efficient markets.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But also, to prevent excessive concentration of influence over information.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If left unchecked, high levels of concentration in media markets may result not only in economic dominance but also in gatekeeping power over what information reaches the public.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this context, the Bill's strengthening of competition oversight is particularly in relation to ownership, control and market conduct and this is both timely and necessary.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, the Bill reflect the Government's responsiveness to industry feedback and its willingness to refine legislation to better reflect market realities, particularly in the media services sector.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: One significant amendment, for example, is the treatment of anti-competitive agreements.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This represents a more calibrated and commercially sensible approach to competition enforcement.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The Bill, however, focuses on traditional media companies, publishers and broadcasters.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: My question is therefore whether there is a possibility of an expanded scope of the Bill – that is, regulating content creation companies that do not fit within the traditional entities that are regulated by the IMDA Act.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We are witnessing the rapid rise of digital and social media ecosystems where news and current affairs content are increasingly consumed online through non-traditional channels such as social media.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Indeed, audiences, particularly younger ones, rely heavily on news outlets, like Mothership, to receive news.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: What we are seeing is the emergence of local companies that are media producers and content-driven businesses that do not necessarily operate traditional newspapers or broadcast channels.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They, nevertheless, produce and disseminate large volumes of content that are consumed and trusted by the masses.

speaker: Ms Cassandra Lee (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet, they may not always fall neatly within the categories of regulated persons under existing legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I will address Members' comments in four broad themes: first, the scope of powers in this Bill and considerations that will guide the Government in exercising these powers; second, the benefits to consumers from fairer, more competitive market conduct; third, the implications on the workforce; and fourth, how this Bill facilitates the growth and development of our media sector, including smaller and diverse players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As Mr Sharael Taha noted in his speech, this Bill is not about content regulation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is also not about the quality of content.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Instead, it focuses on market structures and practices, and consumer protection measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is to ensure fair access and to keep the market vibrant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: While Members are entitled to have different views on the quality of our media entities and the quality of content that they produce, these are not pertaining to the amendments in this Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: But let me just make a few points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Today, mainstream media outlets are trusted and have worked hard to hold their own against much larger global players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A 2025 survey by the Reuters Institute found that our mainstream media outlets remained the most trusted news brands in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We have access to an ever-expanding range of content and media services from global online and streaming platforms, and often consume media from multiple sources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, our local media outlets for news, current affairs, entertainment are working hard to hold their own.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I am proud to say that they are doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: My second point is I think there was confusion about the scope of the Bill, about market structures and concepts of competition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These fundamental approaches and principles cut across many sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is not just telecommunications, it is not just media, but also energy, power, financial services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Competition and consumer protection matters arise across many other sectors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I do not believe that the Members would disagree with the merits of adopting good practices from the telecommunication sector, as well as any other sector, so as to strengthen our regulatory toolkit in the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This Bill reinforces our longstanding commitment to keep Singapore a business-friendly and attractive place for investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We have always exercised our regulatory powers proportionately and fairly, with appropriate checks and balances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And beyond IMDA's regulatory remit, there is also recourse to the Courts through judicial review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is precisely this measured and judicious approach to regulation that has underpinned Singapore's positions as a digital hub, with strong international connectivity and sustained investments by leading global companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And we work hard to make sure that we maintain this reputation globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We can direct regulatees, we can pass regulations, but we cannot force people to invest here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And maintaining that regulatory professionalism and our trusted reputation as pro-business, with regulators that are professional, unbiased and objective, is important.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: That sets the context in which I will try to answer some of the questions from different Members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members have asked about the scope of certain defined terms in the Bill and emphasised the importance of ensuring that the new powers introduced are exercised judiciously, transparently and on a clear basis, so that we maintain a fair and pro-innovation environment and ensure business certainty.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling, Mr Fadli Fawzi, Dr Hamid Razak, Mr David Hoe, Mr Lee Hong Chuang, Mr Andre Low, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Yip Hon Weng raised these points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: At this juncture, Sir, I just want to also note that Ms Mariam Jaafar was unfortunately unable to speak on this Bill because she had to rush to the airport for an overseas work trip.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: She sent to me her speech in advance before she left for the airport so that I can take note of her comments and points.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Where appropriate, I will address her points in my speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They mirror existing definitions in the Telecommunications Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These definitions support our objective of ensuring fair market competition and prevent abuse of market dominance, as I have outlined earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I say that because I think there was some confusion to think we are no longer publishing in the Gazette.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are, but in addition to that, we are publishing on IMDA's website and sending the notification directly to the affected party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is to be more pro-industry because, Sir, unfortunately, not all global companies and investors pay attention to our Government Gazette all the time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, we put it on IMDA's website so that affected parties know about it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Interested parties, licensees included, can refer to them on IMDA's website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, that is the intent of the change.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will engage the owner and controller of such essential resources before the official designation and inform them of such designation by serving notice on them and also publishing on our website, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is the same practice for the telecommunications sector for similar designations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are adopting it for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how the updated definition of "regulated person" will be applied in practice to avoid over-capture beyond key media entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As I shared earlier at the start of my speech, the scope of the powers articulated in this Bill and the regulatory intent remain unchanged.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The definition continues to be targeted at key media entities and only covers entities specified by the Minister in the Gazette.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The updated definition is meant to fill potential gaps in coverage as the market evolves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Really, the Bill aims to target large players that are dominant and to make sure they do not abuse their dominance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is for large entities, key media entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As I explained in my Second Reading speech yesterday, there may be key media entities which may fall outside the existing definition of "regulated person" in the IMDA Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, the amendments are aligned with the approach for the telecommunication sector, for example, in capturing business trust structures, which is a fairly recent corporate structure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Therefore, this power is neither a catch-all nor unconstrained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Under the new section 61A(4), IMDA is required to give prior written notice to the person concerned except where it considers not practicable or desirable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In stating the proposed direction and its effect, IMDA allows for representations to be made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: IMDA must then consider these representations fully before deciding whether to issue the direction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: A similar power already exists under the Telecommunications Act and is intended to address scenarios where a party, for example, provides false or misleading information or documents to IMDA in order to obtain IMDA's approval.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Yip asked about the proportionate exercise of IMDA's information gathering powers in the new sections 65B and 71A.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The Bill specifies that these are to enable IMDA to obtain information relating to the holding of equity interest and control of voting power in a regulated person and information relating to a media resource where IMDA has reason to believe that it should be designated as an essential resource respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, it is constrained and it is read in that context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Dr Choo, Mr Fadli, Mr Lee Hong Chuang, Mr Low, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Sharael and Ms Jessica Tan had questions on the exercise of powers under the new section 69A, which allows the Minister to order structural separations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We fully recognise the gravity and impact of separation orders on affected entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: To this end, this power has strict legal limits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: First, there must be a qualifying market condition.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Either the regulated person owns a media resource so costly to replicate that it blocks competitors from entering the market or the regulated person holds significant market power and competitors cannot realistically provide media services without access to their services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Second, a separation order cannot be invoked by the Minister unless conventional regulatory remedies by IMDA have already been exhausted or are demonstrably inadequate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Third, the Minister must be independently satisfied that issuing the separation order is in the public interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In making this assessment on public interest, the Minister is required to work within the confines of the law and consider whether the order is necessary or desirable to promote fair and efficient competition in the media sector, to enhance the efficiency and international competitiveness of Singapore's media industry, to eliminate or reduce barriers to competition arising from the regulated person's ownership or market power, or to promote transparency, non-discrimination and equivalence of supply in the provision of media services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Even after deciding to issue an order, the Minister's discretion remains constrained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The new section 69A(4) will require the Minister to ensure that the specific directions included in the separation order are proportionate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In assessing proportionality, the Minister must consider how contestable the relevant media services market is and whether the directions will effectively eliminate or minimise any incentive or opportunity for the regulated person to distort competition in that market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: All of these legal requirements must be satisfied and no single requirement alone is sufficient.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This reflects a clear legislative intent: a separation order is a last resort.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Precisely because this is a serious intervention, it is important that the necessary powers are available should the situation arises.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Their existence also send a strong signal to the market that the Government will act decisively to safeguard fair competition and market conduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This, in turn, helps deter abusive market behaviour before it takes hold.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: That discussion underscored the need for us to be prepared for future uncertainties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The powers to issue separation orders are framed in the same spirit, to ensure that we are not caught unprepared in addressing significant market risks should they emerge.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I have also said in my Second Reading speech that it is appropriate for a decision of this gravity to be taken at the Ministerial level.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In addition, this process is also amenable to judicial review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: At the same time, we recognise that acquisitions, mergers or consolidations may generate economies of scale or introduce innovation, with potential pro-competitive effects and consumer benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These considerations will be assessed against our primary objective of maintaining competitive markets that protect consumer interests as part of the broadened oversight of major acquisitions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Dr Choo, Mr Fadli and Mr Hoe asked about the intent, design considerations behind both the reconsideration and appeal mechanisms, including if there could be room for independent review.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This reconsideration process allows parties to ask IMDA to review decisions if new information or considerations arise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The appeal mechanism provides process flexibility, allowing parties to choose whether to appeal directly to the Minister or seek reconsideration first.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The provisions for both processes, including the timeline, process and requirements are stated clearly in the new sections 67A and 68.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Sometimes, the parties may want for IMDA to reconsider the decision because new material information has come up.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, it gives the parties an additional option to seek the regulator's reconsideration rather than directly appealing to the Minister in the first instance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, it is an additional option, but parties can still decide to go straight to the Minister for appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It is meant to be pro-industry and also facilitate timely resolution of issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members should also note that appeals to Minister are independently assessed from IMDA's regulatory decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Taken together, this framework provides multiple levels of checks and safeguards for a regulatory decision, including review by the Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As mentioned, the Minister also needs to be accountable to the public and to this House, to Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Yip asked how both public and industry interests would be considered under the new section 61, where IMDA can approve documents prepared by a person other than IMDA as a code of practice or standard of performance for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The amendments provide additional flexibility for IMDA to benefit industry players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: If there are codes of practice or standards of performance by others that meet IMDA's regulatory requirements, there should not be a need for IMDA to "reinvent the wheel".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It saves time and resources for all stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: IMDA will consult industry and the public before issuing any new codes, as its current practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Broadly, Dr Choo, Mr Fadli, Mr Hoe and Ms Jessica Tan, also raised the importance of transparency in the exercise of powers under the Bill, to both industry and the public.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Generally, written notice will be issued to the affected party ahead of regulatory decisions and there are opportunities for the party to make representations, to then be considered by IMDA or the Minister before they decide.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We intend to inform the public when major regulatory decisions are made, given their impact on the media landscape and to explain the key considerations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I would also make clear that notifications by IMDA on matters, such as the specification of essential resources will continue to be published on the Gazette for information, in addition to other channels, like on our website and direct notifications to the affected party.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are committed to being open and transparent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is a reputation that we build up, over years and decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The litmus test is the business community, global investors, international players wanting to invest in Singapore and continuing to invest in Singapore, because they trust the Government, they trust the regulatory environment and they trust the professionalism and transparency of our processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As per usual practice, IMDA has published the response received on IMDA's website.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I took a look at it, it is a three- or four-page paper by a law firm.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I looked through the details of it before and I looked at it again because Mr Low raised it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The submission had broadly raised the same points that many of the Members suggested, to more clearly define key terms, such as "essential resources" and also noting similar comments on the phrasing of section 61A, which confers powers on IMDA to issue directions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These comments are similar to what many Members had raised, and I believed have addressed them in my Opening speech of the Second Reading as well as my Closing speech.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: So, rest assured, before any major decisions are taken, we consult, we take a look very carefully at what responders have provided to us and look at what their suggestions are.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: On the exercise of powers, MDDI shares Members' commitment to ensuring these powers are exercised properly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Members can be assured that the same rigour and care will apply in this context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Dr Hamid Razak, Mr David Hoe, Ms Mariam Jaafar, and Mr Yip Hon Weng noted that the amendments should translate into benefits for consumers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These amendments in this Bill aim to do so by strengthening the regulatory framework for the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The amendments proposed in this Bill help ensure that Singapore's media market remains competitive, dynamic and fair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: They contribute to public confidence in the media sector, good content, reasonable prices and a vibrant information environment for every Singaporean.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Ms Cassandra Lee asked whether the Government is considering further developments to the regulation of social media use by adolescents, in the context of increasing use of such platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are deeply concerned about ensuring a trusted and safe online environment for everyone and we approach this on many fronts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Over the years, we have introduced various laws to ensure that Singaporeans go online safely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These Codes require the designated services to put in place systems and processes to mitigate their users' risks of exposure to harmful content on their platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Earlier in this Sitting, on 5 May, we have also answered questions on the regulation of social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As the amendments of this Bill do not pertain to these specific matters, I would refer Ms Lee to those replies and to raise subsequent Parliamentary Questions if needed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Mr Yip Hon Weng spoke about the workforce impact and the need to support workers during organisational changes from mergers or restructurings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We recognise the disruptions and anxiety that workers may face and the importance of whole-of-Government oversight of such shifts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I would stress that while the amendments in the Bill focus on fair markets and consumer protection in the media sector, that does not mean that we are not supporting our workers through disruptions and transitions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: MOM's legislative frameworks and guidelines that are broad-based and applied across the various industry sectors will continue to be in force.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: For MDDI and IMDA, in dealing with the telecommunication and media sectors, we encourage unionised companies embarking on or undergoing major organisational restructurings to engage the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and their unions early, and work closely with them to manage the impact on staff.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We will also work closely with NTUC and unions in the telecommunication and media sectors to support affected members during those periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Importantly, we are not passively waiting for disruption to happen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: IMDA actively partners with NTUC and unions to train and skill our workers, so that they remain relevant and competitive in the fast-changing telecommunications and media sectors that are being transformed by AI.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Mr David Hoe, Ms Mariam Jaafar, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Mr Andre Low asked whether the Bill facilitates an open and diverse media landscape with independent perspectives, where new entrants can grow and compete in a fair market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Ms Cassandra Lee also asked if we would update our competition framework to include non-traditional media entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The regulated persons under the IMDA Act are intended to be specific entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: These include major players, including SPH Media Trust, Mediacorp and our Pay TV operators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: We are not making changes to this approach.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In this context, as I emphasised earlier, the regulatory focus of the IMDA Act is not on the smaller players in the media sector and media consumption is non-exclusive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: Singaporeans have access to a wide variety of content and media services through global online and streaming platforms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: The amendments in this Bill are related to ownership and control, and are scoped to cover very specific regulated key media entities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And we certainly recognise that the media landscape has transformed and grown significantly with the internet and social media.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: This is a fast-moving space and we will continue to monitor developments closely.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I would also like to add that IMDA wears a number of hats.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In addition from a regulator point of view, it also plays a role of the media industry developer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: It has put in place schemes and programmes to support local players and grow the diversity and vibrancy of our media ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: And we will continue to do more to support our local media players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: (In Mandarin):   Today's amendment Bill draws on good practices from the telecommunication sector to ensure more effective regulation, promote fair competition and continue safeguarding consumer interests in the media sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In a rapidly evolving media environment, it is important to ensure that our regulatory framework remains effective and forward-looking.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: As Mr Lee Hong Chuang has noted, any new regulatory measures must be proportionate to the issues – neither excessive nor inadequate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: I also agree with Dr Choo Pei Ling that we must remain transparent in our approach to regulation, so as to ensure that industry players and the public continue to have confidence in our regulatory framework.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information (Mr Tan Kiat How)
text: In a rapidly evolving media landscape, it is important that our regulatory framework remains effective and forward looking.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have several clarifications for Senior Minister of State Tan.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Sorry, I have not counted them, so I seek your forgiveness for that.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The other law firm had published an article on the website, but had not directly responded to the consultation.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I appreciate that the Senior Minister of State has responded in broad terms that the scope of the legislation is meant to cover large players, key players in the middle media landscape.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And subsequently, he also confirmed that the intent is not to address the small players.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I asked this because now, you hear about podcasts being acquired for hundreds of millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, it is well within conception that podcasts might well fall under a type of company or entity that may need to be regulated under these provisions.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also had a specific concern about the "in the public interest" line, in section 61A, para 1C.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I appreciate that Senior Minister of State Tan has clarified that this needs to be read in the context of the full provision, so it is not meant to be a catch-all.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would just like to add that the drafting in the Bill is quite vague, because in para B(2), which immediately precedes the phrasing of "in the public interest", it ends with an "or".

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, if you read that together in context, it does seem like 61A(1), para C is meant to be read independently.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if it is read independently, it can seem like a broad all-encompassing power to direct "in the public interest".

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I also have a specific question on the newspaper permit, and similarly for the broadcasting permit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If you read section 69A (3)b(ii) of the Bill, it seems to imply that companies that have been subject to a separation order will be obligated to reapply for their newspaper licence or broadcasting licence as the case may be.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I wonder why it does not just transfer, as a matter of course; and is this an opportunity for the Government to then subsequently deny the successor entity a newspaper or broadcasting licence?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think that covers the scope of my clarifications.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would just finally add that I still have some overarching concerns about the potential for this Bill to have a chilling effect.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think the Senior Minister of State Tan has mentioned that investor confidence in Singapore is broadly high, and I accept that point.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I think specifically for the media industry, Singapore's media industry is currently – I would not say it is a bastion of a free and open market.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We are dominated by two major media companies that are within the Government's orbit.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, I would push back on that suggestion that within the media landscape, that investors have high confidence investing in Singapore companies.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I ask the Member to let me know if I have missed out some things.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, it is about the scope of definitions of regulated persons under the IMDA Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The regulatory intent is clear; and when you read the different provisions and amendments, it should be in the context of the scope of powers envisaged under this Act and debated here in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And that was the IMDA Act that was passed some time ago.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And that overarching intent should be one guiding how we interpret the different clauses and provisions and powers in the Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, the exercise of these powers, whether through the regulator, like IMDA, or in certain circumstances, by the Minister, it should be read in a context of how it will enable better fair market competition and protect the consumers, especially against large players who abuse the position of dominance.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, whether it is articulation of the clause of "public interest", or in terms of thinking of who are the regulated persons defined under the Act, it should be seen in that context – larger players that may abuse their dominance to frustrate new entrants.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: That is really the thrust of the IMDA Act – market structures, market practices, consumer protection.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And nothing in this amendment Act changes the other Acts that govern the media sector, whether the Newspaper and Printing Presses Act or the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I just wanted to be very clear how we should interpret the provisions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: That is important because our exchange here will be in the Hansard and will be relied on if there are further challenges in the courts or elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I just want to make that point very clear.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, that is on scope, definition, public interest.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As for the specific scenario of transferee selection in the event of a structural separation order and why, under the Act, it is envisaged that the entity may have to apply for a newspaper licence at a point in time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I took some time in my opening Second Reading speech, as well as the closing speech, to articulate that structural separation orders by the Minister is not to be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is not just about the telecommunication or media sector, where these powers are now embedded.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But it sends a broader signal to the global investment community, the international businesses – many of them international businesses, listed companies.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Many, many options of not just investing in Singapore, many places for them to invest.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And these are large companies with robust corporate governance, institutional investors, shareholders; and they look at where to invest their resources, their money.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Our regulatory certainty and pro-business environment gives us the competitive advantage.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is not something to be taken lightly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is a reputation that we husband, we shepherd, we safeguard.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, that is really one context in how we think about structural separation orders.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, these decisions are not taken lightly at all.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: With that as a context, let me go into next point.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Member was talking about a hypothetical example or situation where a separation order has been issued, what happens?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Well, it is a lot of conjecture and hypothetical scenarios, because we have not even envisaged a scenario where it will happen and we have not yet exercised such powers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But most importantly, it is really in the exercise of such powers and the next level of details.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Does it protect consumer interest?" And that should guide the decisions of the structures after that.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Those structures also need to involve the affected parties who are receiving the direction.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And the affected parties may be large companies with their own shareholders, their own set of investors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These issues need to be talked through and discussed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I think at that point in time, if they need to apply for licences, if they need apply for a permit to operate, they should do so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The same criteria to evaluate any permit application are already embedded in the existing laws and regulations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I hope that explains the context to Mr Low.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Senior Minister of State, in his wrapping-up speech, referred to a speech made by a Member who did not deliver a speech in Parliament on the Bill, that is, hon Member Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would just like to confirm whether that is as per the Standing Orders of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Because on the Hansard, we will not have the hon Member's speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Senior Minister of State has referred to her, I believe, at least once at the beginning and once in the course of his speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: First, a Member has to be present to make his or her speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, her speech that Senior Minister of State Tan referred to will definitely not be in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any Member who wishes to make a point must be in Parliament to make his or her speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: This is a good reminder to all Members that you have to be present in the Chamber to make your speech and make your points.
